The Smoot-Hawley Act of 1930, which imposed increased tariffs on 20,000 items over four years, resulted in a two-thirds drop in world trade, a 90 percent drop in the Dow Jones Industrial Average, and a 45 percent drop in nominal U.S. GDP. According to many economists and historians, the Great Depression of the 1930s also contributed to the rise of far-right groups in Europe and helped bring Hitler to power and ultimately to World War II. Initially, however, there was little sign of such dire consequences. The "noble" goal of the Smoot-Howley Act was to protect American farmers (at that time 25% of Americans were farmers) from the influx of cheaper food from Europe. And this was still the result of World War I - in the years 1915-19 food prices rose sharply, encouraging Americans to take out loans to maintain and grow crops and to pay for field leases. However, after the end of the war on the Old Continent, the situation slowly stabilized, crops returned to their previous sizes, and grain prices fell. Indebted farmers were unable to compete with European farmers and already in 1922, a law was passed in the USA imposing an average import tax of 40%. The law of 1930 went further and increased tariffs on 20,000 goods by another 40-48%. Initially, it was to protect sugar producers, but soon the act expanded - each senator wanted to act as a "defender" of the interests of his state. Edgar Hoover signed the bill (despite a letter of protest signed by over 1,000 economists!). At that time, the Dow Jones had already fallen to 226 points, and the bottom fell two years later at around 40 points ? almost 90% below the peak. The Dow Jones Industrial Average did not make up for these losses until 1954. Why U.S. Consumers Will Bear the Biggest Burden from Tariffs on Canada and Mexico

The 25% tariffs on Canadian and Mexican imports imposed by the U.S. will hurt American consumers and businesses more than Canada or Mexico. The key reasons are geographical constraints, supply chain integration, and transportation costs.

1. Canada and Mexico Are the U.S.'s Primary Trade Partners

Canada and Mexico account for nearly 30% of all U.S. imports.

Canada alone supplies 77% of its exports to the U.S., meaning the U.S. relies heavily on Canadian goods?especially raw materials like steel, aluminum, and lumber.

The U.S. has imposed tariffs on both neighbors, forcing importers to seek alternative suppliers in Europe, Asia, or South America?all of which come with significant downsides.

2. Replacing Canada & Mexico with Overseas Suppliers is Unrealistic

If U.S. importers had cheaper, high-quality alternatives outside North America, they would already be using them.

U.S. businesses prefer Canada and Mexico because of: 

Lower transportation costs due to proximity.

Just-in-time supply chains, which depend on quick deliveries (impossible with overseas shipping).

Trade agreements and regulatory similarities making cross-border commerce easier.

Finding new suppliers isn¡¯t just costly?it¡¯s impractical in industries like automobiles, aerospace, and construction, where North American supply chains have been optimized for decades.

3. Transportation Costs Alone Will Erase Any "Cost Savings" from Tariffs

Shipping from Europe or Asia is far more expensive than a 25% tariff on Canadian/Mexican goods.

Example: A 40-foot container from China or Europe to the U.S. costs $8,000?$12,000 in shipping alone, depending on fuel prices and congestion.

For bulky goods like steel, aluminum, and lumber, ocean freight adds 30-50% to costs, making Canadian and Mexican imports cheaper even with tariffs.

4. Higher Consumer Prices Across Multiple Sectors

Since Canadian and Mexican imports are deeply embedded in U.S. industries, tariffs will raise costs for:

Construction: Lumber and steel prices will increase, raising home prices.

Automobiles: Car production costs will rise since parts come from all three North American countries.

Consumer Goods: Everything from appliances to groceries will see price hikes due to higher raw material and shipping costs.

Energy: Canada supplies 60% of U.S. crude oil imports. Tariffs on energy imports will increase gas prices, hurting consumers and businesses.

5. U.S. Businesses Will Struggle, Leading to Job Losses

Manufacturers will pay more for raw materials, forcing them to either raise prices or cut costs by reducing jobs.

Small businesses will be hit hardest since they lack the resources to absorb tariff-related price hikes.

Industries that depend on exports (like agriculture and aerospace) will suffer due to Canadian/Mexican retaliation tariffs, further squeezing American businesses.

6. Canada and Mexico Have Other Options ? The U.S. Does Not

Canada and Mexico will diversify their trade partners, increasing exports to Europe and Asia.

The U.S. does not have neighboring trade partners to replace Canada and Mexico.

U.S. consumers will not have an alternative to higher prices because everything?whether imported from far away or produced domestically?will cost more.

Conclusion: U.S. Consumers and Businesses Will Suffer the Most

The 25% tariffs on Canadian and Mexican goods will backfire on the U.S., leading to:
? Higher prices for everyday goods.
? Job losses in key industries.
? Disruptions in supply chains that took decades to build.
? Higher transportation costs that exceed any "savings" from shifting suppliers.

By imposing these tariffs, the U.S. is effectively taxing its own consumers while forcing importers into higher-cost alternatives. Canada and Mexico will adjust over time, but American consumers will be left paying the bill.

Alternative supply, substitutes and increased supply resulting from increased prices will all factor in.  It all works out in the wash and ultimately results in far less impact that might otherwise be expected relative to the magnitude of the tariff increases.  It would be best if there were no tariffs, but it's not a level playing field and most of the U.S's trading partners already have higher tariffs on imports from the U.S. than the U.S. has on imports from those partners.   There's definitely some need for adjustments.  The oil sector will probably be the least impacted area since U.S. production has been artificially reduced over the past four years and is positioned to rapidly increase domestic production.   The Chinese tariffs will result in substantial movement to other low cost sources, especially in S.E. Asia.  There will be, after adjustments, some upward increase on prices for some goods, but not inflation...unless, of course, the tariff rates are continually increased.  You might see a 6 month or so period with some upward price pressure, but after that prices will stabilize at some point well below the increases of the tariffs, cetibus parabus, varying among goods depending on the availability of alternate sources and substitutes,  and the price elasticity of demand for each product.   Considering the significance of U.S. exports to Mexico, Canada's and China's overall economy and the relative low contribution to the overall U.S. economy of imports from the same, in most sectors and for most products, the economic and political impacts will be far more significant on the U.S. partners than on the U.S.  And there are other U.S. trade partners who will benefit from these tariffs who will be eager to benefit thereby.  Overall the U.S. has far more leverage here than Mexico, Canada and China.    I've heard a lot of chatter about "avocados" for example.  This is actually a pretty good example.  Initially U.S. prices will increase (probably by more than the impact on import prices due to the tariff, because "markets always over-react").  The quantity of demand for avocados will resultingly fall.   Prices will fluctuate a bit as prices begin to follow the actual cost increases, and will then stabilize at some portion of the tariff increase above the prior prices.  Then alternate sources will begin to enter the market.  Ultimately prices will end up at a level higher than the pre-tariff level, but substantially below 25% more than previously.  And U.S. consumers will simply consume 5-10% less avocados, at prices 5-10% higher than previously.   The impacts on Mexican avocado growers and shippers will be somewhat more substantial and alternate growers will reap a windfall.   It's not a bad 'example' of the way it will all work out.   There will be some increased domestic production, but the 5-10% increase in prices won't likely result in a large domestic production increase, simply because the demand isn't high enough to cover relatively expensive legal U.S. labor.  Those producers who can substitute automation for labor will however get the lions share of whatever increased revenue is available to domestic producers.  It is worth noting that since this is an agricultural sector product, fluctuations in price from other factors beyond human control, will, as always, impact prices far more than any marginal change in tariffs.

History of Tariffs in the United States 
Tariffs have played a major role in U.S. economic policy since the nation's founding. They have been used to raise revenue, protect domestic industries, and retaliate in trade disputes.

 Early U.S. Tariffs (1789?1860s) ? Revenue & Protection
? Tariff of 1789 ? The first major U.S. tariff under President George Washington. It raised money for the federal government and protected American industries.
? Tariff of 1816 ? The first protective tariff aimed at supporting U.S. manufacturing after the War of 1812.
? Tariff of Abominations (1828) ? A high tariff (up to 62%) that angered Southern states and led to the Nullification Crisis with South Carolina.
? Morrill Tariff (1861) ? Increased tariffs to fund the Civil War, shifting the U.S. toward protectionism.

 Industrial Era & High Tariffs (1865?1930s)
? McKinley Tariff (1890) ? Raised tariffs to an average of 50%, benefiting industrialists but hurting farmers.
? Underwood Tariff (1913) ? Lowered tariffs under President Woodrow Wilson and introduced the income tax to replace lost revenue.
? Smoot-Hawley Tariff (1930) ? Raised tariffs during the Great Depression, worsening global trade and economic collapse.

 Mid-20th Century ? Shift to Free Trade (1940s?1990s)
? Reciprocal Trade Agreements Act (1934) ? Allowed the U.S. to negotiate tariff reductions with other countries.
? GATT (1947) ¡æ WTO (1995) ? The U.S. helped establish the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT), later becoming the World Trade Organization (WTO), reducing global tariffs.
? NAFTA (1994) ? The North American Free Trade Agreement eliminated tariffs between the U.S., Canada, and Mexico.

 21st Century ? Tariff Wars & Trade Policy Shifts
? China Tariffs (2018?2020) ? Under President Donald Trump, the U.S. imposed tariffs on $370 billion worth of Chinese goods. China retaliated with tariffs on U.S. exports.
? USMCA (2020) ? Replaced NAFTA, keeping low tariffs but adding stricter trade rules.
? Biden Administration (2021?Present) ? Maintained many Trump-era tariffs, especially against China, but eased some for European allies.

 U.S. Tariff Trends Over Time
1789?1913: High tariffs (main source of government revenue).
1913?1945: Lower tariffs (shift to income tax, global trade agreements).
1945?2000s: Free trade era (GATT, WTO, NAFTA).
2018?Present: Tariff wars & protectionism return (China, steel, aluminum).
? Final Takeaways
 The U.S. originally used tariffs for revenue but later for industry protection & trade policy.
 High tariffs dominated the 19th & early 20th centuries, but free trade increased after WWII.
 Recent years have seen a return to protectionism, especially with China.

Both Britain and the United States believed the Tariff Act would drive Canada to join the United States.  In reality, it had the complete opposite result.  The Tariff Act instead pushed Canada to align itself more with Britain.  The Conservative Prime Minister Macdonald used the tariffs as a rallying cry in the 1891 election and was able to win another majority government.  Within two years of the Tariff Act being passed, agricultural exports to Britain from Canada tripled and produce and animal exports to Britain grew by 50%.

American consumers dealt with a sharp increase in prices. The Republicans lost the 1890 Congressional elections, losing 93 seats while the Democrats gained 86. How the act affected the economy

It reduced the amount of goods exported from the U.S. 
It led to retaliatory tariffs from other countries, which further reduced global trade. 
It contributed to bank failures, especially in agricultural areas. 
Why the act was passed
The act was intended to protect American businesses and farmers from foreign competition. However, economists warned against the act, and the stock market reacted negatively to its passage. 
Impact on the Great Depression

1. Global Wage Disparities

    Labor Cost Differences: Wages vary significantly between countries due to differences in economic development, cost of living, productivity, and labor market conditions. For example, wages in developing countries are often much lower than in developed countries like the U.S.

    Outsourcing and Offshoring: Many U.S. companies outsource production to countries with lower labor costs to reduce expenses and increase profits. This practice has contributed to wage stagnation in some U.S. industries while creating jobs in lower-wage countries.

2. Globalization and Free Trade

    Comparative Advantage: Countries often specialize in producing goods or services where they have a comparative advantage (e.g., lower labor costs, abundant resources). This can lead to lower wages in certain sectors as countries compete in the global market.

    Trade Agreements: Free trade agreements (e.g., NAFTA, now USMCA) can encourage countries to keep wages low to attract foreign investment and remain competitive in export markets. However, these agreements are often negotiated with mutual benefits in mind, not solely to enrich the U.S.

3. Role of Multinational Corporations

    Profit Maximization: Multinational corporations, including those based in the U.S., often seek to minimize costs by operating in countries with lower wages. This can put downward pressure on wages globally as countries compete to attract investment.

    Exploitation Concerns: In some cases, low wages in developing countries are the result of exploitative labor practices, weak labor laws, and poor enforcement. While this benefits corporations and consumers in wealthier countries, it often comes at the expense of workers in lower-wage countries.

4. Impact on U.S. Workers

    Wage Stagnation: The outsourcing of jobs to lower-wage countries has contributed to wage stagnation and job losses in certain U.S. industries, particularly manufacturing.

    Consumer Benefits: Lower wages abroad can lead to cheaper goods for American consumers, but this often comes at the cost of reduced job opportunities and wage growth for U.S. workers.

5. Resistance and Pushback

    Labor Movements: In many countries, workers and labor unions are fighting for higher wages and better working conditions, challenging the status quo of low wages.

    Government Policies: Some governments are implementing policies to raise minimum wages, improve labor standards, and reduce income inequality.

    Shift in Global Supply Chains: Rising wages in countries like China are leading some companies to relocate production to other low-wage countries or even back to the U.S. through reshoring.

6. Broader Economic Forces

    Automation and Technology: Advances in technology and automation are also impacting wages and employment worldwide, often reducing the need for low-skilled labor.

    Global Inequality: The global economic system is characterized by significant inequality, with wealth and power concentrated in a few countries and corporations. This system can perpetuate low wages in developing countries while benefiting wealthier nations.

Conclusion

While it¡¯s true that wage disparities and globalization have contributed to economic dynamics that benefit the U.S. and other wealthy nations, the idea that every country is deliberately lowering wages to make America rich is an oversimplification. In 1890, the Tariff Act came into place in the United States. It placed tariffs on imports of up to 50%.
While touted as a way to build American industry, there was also the hope it would force an annexation of Canada. It backfired.
Let's learn more.
Put forward by William McKinley, who was a Congressman at that point, the Tariff Act put duties across imports ranging from 38% to 49.5%.
McKinley was called the Napoleon of Protection. While some items had tariffs eliminated, most had tariffs increased.
One reason for the tariffs was to force the annexation of Canada. The McKinley Tariff declined to make an exception for Canadian products.
It was hoped this would make Canada more reliant on the US market, and push Canadians to become the 45th state.
Secretary of State James G. Blaine believed that annexation would eliminate competition with Canada over fishing and timber rights. Blane co-authored the Tariff Act.
He stated of annexation: "a grander and nobler brotherly love, that may unite in the end¡±
British politician Lyon Playfair saw the Tariff Act for what it was. He called it a covert attack on Canada,
Both Britain and the United States believed the Tariff Act would drive Canada to join the United States.
In reality, it had the complete opposite result.
The Tariff Act instead pushed Canada to align itself more with Britain. People began to rally behind their "love for Queen, flag, and country".
Sir John A. Macdonald used the tariffs as a rallying cry in the 1891 election and was able to win another majority government.
Within two years of the Tariff Act being passed, agricultural exports to Britain from Canada went from $3.5 million to $15 million.
Produce and animal exports to Britain grew from $16 million to $24 million during that same period.
Minister of Trade and Commerce Mackenzie Bowell said:
¡°The McKinley Bill, instead of destroying the trade of this country, has only diverted it from the United States to England."
American consumers dealt with a sharp increase in prices.
The Republicans lost the 1890 Congressional elections, losing 93 seats while the Democrats gained 86.
In 1892, the Democrats gained control of the Senate, House and Presidency.
They then replaced the Tariff Act with a new act that lowered tariffs.

It is widely cultivated for food, animal feed, and biofuel production, particularly in Africa, Asia, and the Americas. The grain is rich in carbohydrates, fiber, and protein and is naturally gluten-free, making it popular in gluten-free diets.

Sorghum can be consumed in various forms, such as whole grains, flour for baking, or even popped like popcorn. Some varieties are used for syrup production, while others serve as forage for livestock. It is also an essential ingredient in some alcoholic beverages, such as sorghum beer and baijiu, a Chinese distilled spirit.

Its ability to thrive in arid conditions makes it a crucial staple crop in regions with limited water availability.
